drills.q: State RTL's core philosophy and what happens to a well-written RTL suite when a component is refactored from class-based to hooks with no behavior change.
drills.a: "The more your tests resemble how software is used, the more confidence they give." A well-written suite queries/interacts like a real user and asserts on visible outcomes, so nothing should break from a pure implementation refactor -- if tests do break, they were coupled to implementation details, not following the philosophy.

drills.q: Why does RTL rank getByRole above getByTestId, and when is getByTestId actually appropriate?
drills.a: getByRole queries by accessible role/name, so failure to find an element this way also signals a potential real accessibility gap. getByTestId bypasses that signal and couples the test to an implementation detail. Appropriate only as a genuine last resort when no accessible query can identify the element and improving semantic markup isn't feasible.

drills.q: Why does MSW intercept at the network layer instead of mocking fetch/an API client module, and what gap does this NOT close on its own?
drills.a: Network-layer interception means application code makes a genuinely real request that's intercepted, so the same handlers work across unit, integration, E2E, and local dev -- avoiding duplicated per-test-file fakes. It doesn't close the mock-accuracy gap on its own; handlers can still drift from what the real API returns without a shared contract source or periodic contract tests.

drills.q: What specifically makes Playwright locators auto-waiting, what flakiness class does it eliminate, and what does it NOT eliminate?
drills.a: Locators/assertions retry against live DOM state until the condition is met or timeout, eliminating the historically biggest E2E flake source: asserting before an async update resolves. It does not eliminate shared test state interference or genuine environment/network timing variance.

drills.q: Explain the testing trophy vs the classic testing pyramid, what specific failure mode the trophy reacts to, and whether it means minimizing unit tests.
drills.a: The pyramid puts unit tests as the widest layer; the trophy (Kent C. Dodds) puts integration tests widest, since most real bugs live in connections between units, not isolated functions -- pyramid-shaped suites can have high unit coverage while missing whole bug classes. It doesn't mean eliminating unit tests -- they remain right for algorithmically complex, isolable logic; the trophy argues for proportion, not elimination of any layer.

drills.q: Name the well-documented causes of visual regression test flakiness and their fixes, plus one additional cause beyond OS/GPU rendering and dynamic content.
drills.a: Font rendering/anti-aliasing/sub-pixel positioning differ by OS/GPU -- fix by generating/comparing baselines only in a consistent Docker environment. Dynamic content (timestamps, IDs) -- fix by masking/excluding before comparison. Additional cause: in-progress animations/transitions or content that hasn't fully settled at capture time -- fix with reduced-motion handling or waiting for a stable state before screenshotting.

drills.q: A team's E2E suite is 40 minutes with a 15% flake rate. Diagnose the likely causes in order of typical prevalence and propose a remediation plan.
drills.a: Likely causes: shared/mutable test state causing cross-test interference, too much coverage pushed to the E2E layer instead of integration, and genuine environment/timing variance. Remediation: move non-browser-dependent tests down to RTL+MSW integration, isolate test data per run, parallelize across CI workers, and quarantine/investigate flaky tests rather than letting them be ignored.

drills.q: Why can a test suite be 100% green while a feature is visibly broken in the browser, and can this still happen even with correctly-used RTL?
drills.a: It happens when assertions target implementation details (internal state, DOM structure) that remain true despite broken user-facing behavior. RTL structurally prevents that specific class since it can only assert on visible/operable output -- but a team can still write insufficiently narrow RTL assertions (checking existence without content, or not exercising the actual interaction that triggers a bug), so behavioral coverage still requires deliberate judgment RTL doesn't enforce.

drills.q: A team pushes back that reducing E2E coverage feels like reducing safety. How do you address this directly?
drills.a: Reframe the tradeoff: a suite nobody trusts (routinely re-run on failure or ignored) provides less real safety than a smaller, fast, reliable suite that's actually respected and actionable. Coverage that exists on paper but is dismissed isn't providing the safety it appears to -- the goal is maximizing trusted signal, not test count.

drills.q: MSW mocks pass in CI but the real integration breaks in staging. What's the likely cause and the fix?
drills.a: The mock handler's response shape has silently drifted from what the real API actually returns, since nothing automatically keeps them in sync. Fix: generate MSW handlers from a shared API contract (OpenAPI spec, tRPC types) where possible, or add lightweight contract tests validating the real API against the same shape the mock assumes.
